--- title: "16 · Model-Based Methods" subtitle: "Part III — Model Uncertainty" jupyter: python3 execute: echo: false --- ::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"} **Executed in:** Python · **Book:** ADM Ch. 16 · **Lecture:** to be added ::: ## Big picture ### Where this chapter fits [Chapter 15](ch15-exploration-and-exploitation.qmd) handled a world with a single state: each action paid off with an unknown probability. Now the actions also move the agent between states, and we don't know how. **Model-based** reinforcement learning is the most direct answer: learn the model (the transition and reward functions) from experience, and plan on it with the methods of Chapter 7. This raises three questions. How do we estimate the model? How do we keep the plan up to date as the model changes after every step, without re-solving from scratch? And how do we explore, when the states worth exploring may be far away? [Chapter 17](ch17-model-free-methods.qmd) takes the other road: learning values directly, without a model. **The question:** how can an agent that doesn't know the dynamics learn a model, plan with it, and explore well enough to find what's worth finding? The short answer: **count what happens, and plan on the counts.** The **maximum likelihood** model uses the observed frequencies as probabilities. Planning can be redone in full after each step, or cheaply for a few states, best chosen by **prioritized sweeping**. Planning on the estimate alone doesn't explore, so add exploration: randomly (ε-greedy), by **optimism** about what hasn't been tried enough (**R-MAX**), or **Bayesian**: keep a posterior over models and act on a sample from it (**posterior sampling**). In principle, a Bayesian agent could plan over beliefs about the model (a **Bayes-adaptive MDP**), but that is rarely tractable. ```{dot} //| label: fig-ch16-map //| fig-width: 6.6 //| fig-height: 3.9 //| fig-cap: "Map of this chapter. Experience updates a model; a planner turns the model into values; an exploration rule turns values into actions." //| fig-alt: "Diagram. A grey box, Experience (s, a, r, s′), points with the label count to two blue boxes: Maximum likelihood model (frequencies) and Bayesian model (Dirichlet posterior). The maximum likelihood model points to Planning (full, randomized, prioritized sweeping), which points to Exploration (epsilon-greedy, R-MAX). The Bayesian model points to Posterior sampling (solve a sampled MDP) and to Bayes-adaptive MDP (plan over beliefs; usually intractable). Exploration and posterior sampling point to Act, which points back to Experience." digraph ch16 { rankdir=TB; bgcolor="#fcfcfb"; pad=0.25; nodesep=0.3; ranksep=0.45; node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fillcolor="white", color="#c3c2b7", penwidth=1.2, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=13, fontcolor="#0b0b0b", margin="0.12,0.07"]; edge [color="#52514e", penwidth=1.2, arrowsize=0.7, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11, fontcolor="#52514e"]; exp [label=<Experience
(s, a, r, s′)>, fillcolor="#f0efec"]; ml [label=<Maximum likelihood
frequencies>, fillcolor="#cde2fb", color="#2a78d6"]; bayes [label=<Bayesian model
Dirichlet posterior>, fillcolor="#cde2fb", color="#2a78d6"]; plan [label=<Planning

ε-greedy, R-MAX>]; ps [label=<Posterior sampling
solve a sampled MDP>]; bamdp [label=<Bayes-adaptive MDP
plan over beliefs>]; act [label=<Act>, fillcolor="#f0efec"]; exp -> ml [label="count"]; exp -> bayes [label="count"]; ml -> plan; plan -> explore; bayes -> ps; bayes -> bamdp [label="exact"]; explore -> act; ps -> act; act -> exp [constraint=false]; } ``` ### The key ideas at a glance 1. **Learn the model by counting.** Record how often each action from each state led to each next state, and the rewards received. The **maximum likelihood** estimate of the transition probability is the observed fraction, and the reward estimate is the average reward. With enough data the estimate converges to the truth, but pairs never tried remain unknown. 2. **Replanning as the model changes.** Every step changes the model a little. Solving the whole MDP again (**full update**) is exact but costly. A **randomized update** backs up the state just visited and a few random ones. **Prioritized sweeping** backs up the states whose values are most likely to have changed: the predecessors of states whose values just moved. 3. **Planning on the estimate doesn't explore.** An agent that trusts its estimate never tries what it believes is worse, so it can stay stuck on a small, nearby reward. It needs an exploration strategy, as in Chapter 15, but now exploration may mean *traveling* to a poorly known part of the world. 4. **Optimism: R-MAX.** Pretend every state-action pair tried fewer than $m$ times pays the maximum possible reward forever. The greedy policy then heads straight for whatever is still unknown, near or far, until it is known. The threshold $m$ trades the risk of trusting too few samples against the time spent exploring. 5. **Bayesian models and posterior sampling.** Keep a **Dirichlet** posterior over each state-action pair's next-state distribution: counts plus prior pseudocounts. **Posterior sampling** draws one plausible MDP from the posterior, solves it, and acts on it. Plausibly good but unexplored options sometimes look good in the sample, so they get tried. 6. **The Bayes-optimal answer.** The ideal Bayesian agent plans over (state, belief) pairs, a **Bayes-adaptive MDP**. It trades exploration against exploitation optimally, as the bandit dynamic program of Chapter 15 did, but its belief space is continuous and huge, so it is solved only approximately. ### Vocabulary | Term | Plain meaning | |:---|:---| | Model-based reinforcement learning | Learn the transition and reward functions, then plan on them | | $N(s, a, s')$, $N(s, a)$ | How often $a$ in $s$ led to $s'$, and how often $a$ was tried in $s$ | | $\rho(s, a)$ | Sum of the rewards received for $a$ in $s$ | | Maximum likelihood model | Probabilities and rewards estimated as observed frequencies and averages | | Bellman backup | Recomputing one state's value from its successors' values | | Full, randomized, prioritized updates | Re-solve everything; back up a few random states; back up the most affected states | | R-MAX | Treat under-tried pairs as maximally rewarding, to drive exploration | | Dirichlet distribution | A distribution over probability vectors; the belief about a next-state distribution | | Posterior sampling | Act optimally in a model drawn from the posterior | | Bayes-adaptive MDP | An MDP whose states include the belief about the model | : Terms used on this page. {#tbl-vocab} ### After this chapter you can - Estimate transition and reward functions from experience, by maximum likelihood or with a Dirichlet posterior. - Keep a value function up to date with full, randomized, or prioritized updates, and judge their cost. - Explain why exploiting a learned model can fail, and fix it with ε-greedy, R-MAX, or posterior sampling. - Tune R-MAX's threshold, and explain the trade-off it controls. - Describe the Bayes-adaptive MDP and why posterior sampling is a practical substitute. ## Intuition ::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"} You've moved to a city with an unreliable bus network, and you don't have a map. - **Counting:** you keep a notebook. "Took the 12 from the station: 7 times it went downtown, 3 times it went to the harbor." - **Planning:** with the notebook, you can work out a good route to anywhere you've been. Each new trip changes the notebook, and it's silly to redo every route every day; update the routes the new entry affects. - **Exploring:** if you only ride buses you already know, you never find the fast line across town. You could ride a random bus now and then, assume every unridden route is wonderful until proven otherwise, or imagine one plausible map consistent with your notebook and follow it. ::: Our running example for exploration is a **mountain trail** with six positions, 0 (the trailhead) to 5 (the summit). At the trailhead the hiker can rest, earning a small 0.05 per step (a snack from the car). **Climbing** moves up one position only 35% of the time; 60% of the time the hiker stays put, and 5% of the time slips back. Enjoying the view at the summit earns 1 per step. Walking back down is reliable. With discount 0.95, the best policy is to climb everywhere: worth 8\.13 from the trailhead, against 1\.00 for resting forever. In the long run it earns 0\.857 per step. The agent doesn't know any of this. ### Counting builds the model Try "climb" at position 2 twenty times; if you moved up 7 times, the estimate of $T(3 \mid 2, \text{climb})$ is 7/20. On Hex World, from uniformly random actions, the estimated transition probabilities of the tried pairs are off by a total of 0\.65 per pair after 100 steps and 0\.21 after 3,000 (@fig-ml-hex). See @eq-ml. ### Replan where it matters Solving Hex World's estimated model after every step took 74 Bellman backups per step. Backing up just the state visited and 5 others cost 6 per step. After 100 steps, the random picks left an average value error of 0\.05 (against the model's exact solution). Prioritized sweeping, choosing those backups by where values just changed, left 0\.008 (@fig-planners). See @eq-priority. ### Exploiting a guess gets stuck At first the agent knows nothing. It rests once, earns 0.05, and now resting has a known positive value while climbing looks worthless: it has never paid. An agent that follows its estimate, with 10% random actions, rarely strings together the dozens of lucky climbs needed to see the summit. Only 5% of 20 such runs learned to climb within 2\,000 steps. ### Be optimistic about the unknown R-MAX treats every action tried fewer than $m$ times as if it paid the maximum reward, 1, forever. From the trailhead, "climb" looks wonderful until it has been tried $m$ times; then position 1's actions look wonderful, and so on up the trail. With $m = 10$, 95% of runs learned to climb. With $m = 3$, only 25%: three tries of an action that succeeds 35% of the time often show no progress, and the agent concludes that climbing is hopeless (@fig-rmax-m). See @eq-rmax. ### Sample a plausible world A Bayesian agent keeps, for every position and action, a Dirichlet belief about where it will end up. Posterior sampling draws one plausible trail from those beliefs, plans on it, and acts. An untried climb might, in the sample, lead straight up, so it gets tried. As evidence accumulates, the samples agree with reality. 100% of runs learned to climb, with no exploration parameter to tune (@fig-exploration). See @eq-dirichlet. ### The ideal is too expensive The perfectly Bayesian agent would plan over what it might *learn*: its state includes its belief. That is a **Bayes-adaptive MDP**, the multi-state version of Chapter 15's dynamic program over bandit counts. Its belief space is continuous, so exact solutions are out of reach even for this six-position trail. See @eq-bamdp. ## Formalism ### Maximum likelihood models Count the transitions $N(s, a, s')$ and the reward sums $\rho(s, a)$ (ADM §16.1). With $N(s, a) = \sum_{s'} N(s, a, s')$: ::: {.key-equation data-name="Maximum likelihood model"} $$ \hat T(s' \mid s, a) = \frac{N(s, a, s')}{N(s, a)}, \qquad \hat R(s, a) = \frac{\rho(s, a)}{N(s, a)} $$ {#eq-ml} ::: **In words.** The estimated probability of a transition is how often it happened; the estimated reward is the average reward received. **Term by term.** - $N(s, a)$ counts how often $a$ was taken in $s$. - If $N(s, a) = 0$ there is no data. Here the estimate is $\hat T = 0$ and $\hat R = 0$: the pair looks like a dead end with no reward. A uniform distribution is another common default. - Prior knowledge can be added by starting the counts at nonzero values. **Why it holds.** For the next state, the observations are draws from a categorical distribution. The likelihood $\prod_{s'} T(s')^{N(s, a, s')}$ is maximized, subject to $\sum_{s'} T(s') = 1$, at the observed fractions (a Lagrange multiplier argument). The sample mean is the maximum likelihood estimate of a mean reward. Planning on $(\hat T, \hat R)$ as if it were the truth is called **certainty equivalence**. ### Keeping the plan up to date After each step the model changes, and the value function $U$ should follow (ADM §16.2). All three schemes use the Bellman backup on the estimated model, $U(s) \leftarrow \max_a \big(\hat R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} \hat T(s' \mid s, a) U(s')\big)$: - **Full update:** solve the estimated MDP, for example by value iteration from the current $U$. - **Randomized update:** back up the state just left and $m$ states chosen at random. This is related to R. S. Sutton's Dyna (1991). - **Prioritized sweeping** (A. W. Moore and C. G. Atkeson, *Machine Learning*, 1993): keep a priority queue of states. Back up the state just left, then repeatedly back up the highest-priority state. When a backup changes $U(s)$, raise the priority of every predecessor $s^-$: ::: {.key-equation data-name="Prioritized sweeping priority"} $$ \text{priority}(s^-) \leftarrow \max\Big(\text{priority}(s^-),\ \max_{a^-} \hat T(s \mid s^-, a^-)\, \big|U(s) - u\big|\Big) $$ {#eq-priority} ::: **In words.** When a state's value changes, the states that lead to it probably need updating too, and more urgently if they lead to it often and the change was large. **Term by term.** - $u$ is the value of $U(s)$ before the backup. - $\hat T(s \mid s^-, a^-)$ is how likely the predecessor's action is to reach $s$. - The product bounds how much $s^-$'s backup could change through $s$: a change of $|U(s) - u|$ in one successor moves a lookahead by at most $\gamma \hat T(s \mid s^-, a^-)|U(s) - u|$. - The queue persists from step to step, so work that couldn't be done in one step's budget of $m$ backups is done later. **Why it holds.** Backups where nothing changed do nothing. Changes propagate backward from where the new information arrived, so ordering backups by the size of the incoming change propagates new information fastest per backup. ### Exploration with a learned model Any Chapter 15 strategy works state by state. For example, ε-greedy takes a random action with probability $\varepsilon$, and otherwise $\arg\max_a \hat Q(s, a)$. But random actions explore only nearby. **R-MAX** (R. I. Brafman and M. Tennenholtz, *JMLR*, 2002) modifies the model instead (ADM §16.3): ::: {.key-equation data-name="R-MAX model"} $$ R(s, a) = \begin{cases} r_{\max} & N(s, a) < m \\ \rho(s, a)/N(s, a) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \qquad T(s' \mid s, a) = \begin{cases} \mathbb{1}[s' = s] & N(s, a) < m \\ N(s, a, s')/N(s, a) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$ {#eq-rmax} ::: **In words.** A pair not yet tried $m$ times is modeled as a paradise: it pays the most any action can pay and keeps you there forever. Act greedily on this model. **Term by term.** - $r_{\max}$ is the largest possible reward (1 on the trail). An under-tried pair is then worth $r_{\max}/(1 - \gamma)$, as much as anything can be worth: 20 on the trail. - The self-loop makes that value independent of the unknown dynamics. - Once a pair has $m$ samples, the maximum likelihood estimate replaces the fantasy. - $m$ trades off: too small, and noisy estimates get trusted; too large, and the agent explores long after it could exploit. **Why it holds.** Planning on this model steers the agent toward reachable unknown pairs, however far away, because their value exceeds anything known. Either the agent does near-optimally for the true MDP, or it reaches an unknown pair with substantial probability and learns something. Since there are finitely many pairs, each needing $m$ visits, learning stops after a bounded number of steps. That gives R-MAX its guarantee: near-optimal behavior after a number of mistakes polynomial in the problem size. ### Bayesian models Put a prior on each next-state distribution $\theta_{(s, a)} = T(\cdot \mid s, a)$ (ADM §16.4). The Dirichlet distribution plays for categorical outcomes the role the Beta distribution played for wins and losses in Chapter 15: ::: {.key-equation .famous data-name="Dirichlet posterior"} $$ b(\theta) = \prod_s \prod_a \mathrm{Dir}\big(\theta_{(s,a)} \mid \boldsymbol\alpha(s, a)\big), \qquad \boldsymbol\alpha(s, a) = \boldsymbol\alpha_0 + \mathbf N(s, a), \qquad P(s' \mid s, b, a) = \frac{\alpha(s, a, s')}{\sum_{s''} \alpha(s, a, s'')} $$ {#eq-dirichlet} ::: **In words.** The belief about where each action leads is a Dirichlet whose parameters are the prior pseudocounts plus the observed counts. The predicted probability of each next state is its share of those counts. **Term by term.** - $\mathrm{Dir}(\theta \mid \boldsymbol\alpha)$ has density proportional to $\prod_{s'} \theta_{s'}^{\alpha_{s'} - 1}$ over probability vectors $\theta$. - $\boldsymbol\alpha_0$ is the prior: all ones is uniform over probability vectors. - $\mathbf N(s, a)$ is the vector of observed counts. Observing $s'$ adds 1 to $\alpha(s, a, s')$. - Each component's marginal is a Beta: $\theta_{s'} \sim \text{Beta}(\alpha_{s'}, \sum \alpha - \alpha_{s'})$. - The beliefs for different $(s, a)$ are independent, so the belief factors into a product. **Why it holds.** The Dirichlet is conjugate to the categorical: prior $\prod \theta^{\alpha - 1}$ times likelihood $\prod \theta^{N}$ is $\prod \theta^{\alpha + N - 1}$, another Dirichlet. The predictive probability is the posterior mean of $\theta_{s'}$, which is its share of $\boldsymbol\alpha$ (as with the Beta, Chapter 4). In this page's code, rewards are unknown too. They lie in $[0, 1]$, so each mean reward gets a $\text{Beta}(1 + \rho, 1 + N - \rho)$ belief (fractional counts are fine). The book's version assumes known rewards. ### Bayes-adaptive MDPs The optimal Bayesian agent solves an MDP over pairs $(s, b)$ of state and belief (ADM §16.5). The belief moves deterministically, by Bayes' rule, $b' = \tau(s, b, a, s')$: ::: {.key-equation data-name="Bayes-adaptive Bellman equation"} $$ U^*(s, b) = \max_a \Big(R(s, a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, b, a)\, U^*\big(s', \tau(s, b, a, s')\big)\Big) $$ {#eq-bamdp} ::: **In words.** Value a situation by what you can earn *and* what you will learn: each outcome both moves you and changes your belief, and later decisions use that better belief. **Term by term.** - $P(s' \mid s, b, a)$ is the predictive probability from @eq-dirichlet: the belief averages over models. - $\tau$ updates the counts: $\alpha(s, a, s') \leftarrow \alpha(s, a, s') + 1$. - With a single state this is exactly [the bandit dynamic program of Chapter 15](ch15-exploration-and-exploitation.qmd#bayes-optimal-exploration). - The belief is continuous in general, so exact solution is out of reach. Approximate methods (Chapters 8 and 9) and the POMDP methods of Part IV apply. **Why it holds.** It is the Bellman optimality equation of an MDP with state $(s, b)$ and known dynamics: $s'$ is drawn with the predictive probability, and $b'$ follows deterministically. The unknown model has been folded into the state. ### Posterior sampling Instead of planning over beliefs, draw one model $\theta \sim b$, solve it, and act greedily on its values; update the belief after each step and draw again (ADM §16.6; M. Strens, *ICML*, 2000). There's no exploration parameter. Plausibly good actions are tried because they are optimal in some samples, and their samples stop looking good once data rules that out. It is the multi-state version of Thompson sampling. Drawing a new model after every step, as here and in the book, can make the agent switch plans often; a common variant keeps each sample for a whole episode. ## Worked example ### A hiker's first eight steps The hiker's first eight steps, as (position, action, reward, next position): ::: {#6fed3603 .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=3} | Step | $s$ | $a$ | $r$ | $s'$ | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 0 | climb | 0 | 0 | | 2 | 0 | climb | 0 | 1 | | 3 | 1 | climb | 0 | 1 | | 4 | 1 | climb | 0 | 2 | | 5 | 2 | back | 0 | 1 | | 6 | 1 | back | 0 | 0 | | 7 | 0 | back | 0.05 | 0 | | 8 | 0 | climb | 0 | 1 | : The hiker's log. {#tbl-log} ::: ::: **Maximum likelihood.** "Climb" was tried 3 times at position 0: it stayed once and went up twice. So $\hat T(1 \mid 0, \text{climb}) =$ 0\.667 and $\hat T(0 \mid 0, \text{climb}) =$ 0\.333. At position 1, climbing went nowhere once and up once: 0\.5 and 0\.5. Resting at the trailhead was tried once, paying 0.05, so $\hat R(0, \text{back}) =$ 0\.05. Climbing at positions 2 to 5 was never tried: $\hat T = 0$, $\hat R = 0$. The true climbing probabilities are 0.35 up and 0.6 stay; eight steps can't tell us that. **R-MAX with $m = 3$.** Only (0, climb) has 3 tries, so only it uses the estimate. Every other pair is modeled as a self-loop paying 1 forever, worth $1/(1 - 0.95) = 20$. At the trailhead, resting is still "unknown", worth 20: $Q(0, \text{back}) =$ 20\.00. Climbing uses the estimate: one step of discount, then a third of the time back at position 0 and two thirds at position 1, where everything is still unknown: $Q(0, \text{climb}) = 0.95 \times 20 =$ 19\.00. So R-MAX rests, to finish learning about resting. It is not after the snack; it is after information. **Bayesian, with a uniform prior.** The Dirichlet for (1, climb) has parameters 1 + counts: [1, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1] over positions 0–5. Its predictive probability of moving up to 2 is 0\.250, and of staying 0\.250. With so little data, the prior's six pseudocounts dominate: every position, even the summit, still has predictive probability at least 0\.125. A sample from this posterior can easily put a big jump up the trail, which is what makes posterior sampling explore. ### One prioritized sweep Suppose a backup at position 3 raises $U(3)$ by 2.0. Its predecessors under the estimated model: position 2 with "climb" reaches 3 with estimated probability 0.4; position 4 with "back" always reaches 3; position 3 itself with "climb" stays with probability 0.5. Their priorities rise to $0.4 \times 2 = 0.8$ for position 2, $1.0 \times 2 = 2.0$ for position 4, and $0.5 \times 2 = 1.0$ for position 3. The next backups go to 4, then 3, then 2, each possibly pushing further predecessors onto the queue. ## Interactive ### The hiker's log Replay one run of each method on the trail. The circles are the six positions, each labeled with how often "climb" has been tried there. The arrow under each shows the action the agent currently prefers there, and the orange dot is the hiker. The trace below shows the hiker's position over time. ```{ojs} hiker = FileAttachment("data/ch16-hiker.json").json() viewof hikerMethod = Inputs.select(hiker.methods, {label: "Method", value: "posterior sampling"}) viewof hikerT = Inputs.range([5, hiker.log[hiker.methods[0]].pos.length], {step: 5, value: 100, label: "Step"}) ``` ```{ojs} hikerNow = { const run = hiker.log[hikerMethod]; const snap = run.snaps[hikerT / hiker.every - 1]; const pos = run.pos.slice(0, hikerT); return {snap, pos, here: pos[pos.length - 1], summit: pos.filter(p => p === 5).length}; } md`Step ${hikerT}: the hiker is at position **${hikerNow.here}** and has spent **${hikerNow.summit}** steps at the summit so far. It currently prefers to climb at **${hikerNow.snap.prefer.filter(a => a === 1).length}** of 6 positions.` ``` ```{ojs} //| label: fig-hiker //| fig-cap: "One run of the chosen method on the trail. Top: the six positions (trailhead left, summit right), each labeled with the number of climbs tried there, with the preferred action below (↑ climb, ← back) and the hiker as an orange dot. Bottom: the hiker's position over time." //| fig-alt: "Interactive diagram. Six circles rise from left to right like a trail, each with a count of climbs tried and an arrow below it, up for climb and left for back. An orange dot marks the hiker's position. Below, a line chart of position (0 to 5) against steps. With epsilon-greedy the hiker mostly stays at position 0 and prefers back almost everywhere; with R-MAX (m = 10) and posterior sampling, the counts grow up the trail, the arrows turn to climb, and the trace reaches the summit and stays near it." { const W = 600, sx = i => 60 + i * 96, sy = i => 150 - i * 22; const nodes = d3.range(6).map(i => svg` ${hikerNow.snap.climbs[i]} ${hikerNow.snap.prefer[i] === 1 ? "↑" : "←"} `); // Labels sit below the lowest arrow (trailhead arrow at y = 194). const top = svg``; const trace = Plot.plot({ width: W, height: 170, style: {background: hiker.style.surface, color: hiker.style.ink}, x: {domain: [0, hiker.log[hikerMethod].pos.length], label: "step"}, y: {domain: [0, 5], label: "position", ticks: 6}, marks: [Plot.line(hikerNow.pos.map((p, t) => ({t, p})), {x: "t", y: "p", stroke: hiker.style.blue, curve: "step-after"})] }); return html`
${top}${trace}
`; } ``` ### What does a Dirichlet belief look like? Set the counts observed for one state and action ("climb" at some position): how often it went up, stayed, or slipped. The chart shows the belief about each of the three probabilities (the Dirichlet's marginals, uniform prior), and five probability vectors sampled from it, as posterior sampling would draw them. ```{ojs} viewof nUp = Inputs.range([0, 40], {step: 1, value: 2, label: "Went up"}) viewof nStay = Inputs.range([0, 40], {step: 1, value: 3, label: "Stayed"}) viewof nSlip = Inputs.range([0, 40], {step: 1, value: 0, label: "Slipped"}) ``` ```{ojs} dir = { // Uniform prior: alpha = 1 + counts. Marginal of component i is Beta(alpha_i, sum - alpha_i). const alpha = [1 + nUp, 1 + nStay, 1 + nSlip], total = d3.sum(alpha); const logFact = k => d3.sum(d3.range(1, k + 1), Math.log); // log (k!) for integers const names = ["up", "stay", "slip"]; const xs = d3.range(0.0025, 1, 0.005); const dens = names.flatMap((name, i) => { const a = alpha[i], b = total - alpha[i]; const logB = logFact(a - 1) + logFact(b - 1) - logFact(a + b - 1); // log Beta function return xs.map(x => ({name, x, y: Math.exp((a - 1) * Math.log(x) + (b - 1) * Math.log(1 - x) - logB)})); }); // Dirichlet samples: independent Gamma(alpha_i) draws, normalized (seeded, so the page is stable). const rand = d3.randomLcg(42); const draws = d3.range(5).map(k => { const g = alpha.map(a => d3.randomGamma.source(rand)(a)()); return names.map((name, i) => ({k: `sample ${k + 1}`, name, p: g[i] / d3.sum(g)})); }).flat(); return {alpha, total, dens, draws, names, means: alpha.map(a => a / total)}; } md`Predictive probabilities (posterior means): up **${dir.means[0].toFixed(3)}**, stay **${dir.means[1].toFixed(3)}**, slip **${dir.means[2].toFixed(3)}**.` ``` ```{ojs} //| label: fig-dirichlet //| fig-cap: "The Dirichlet belief about one action's next-state probabilities, from the chosen counts and a uniform prior. Left: the marginal belief about each probability. Right: five probability vectors sampled from the belief." //| fig-alt: "Interactive charts. Left: three density curves over probabilities from 0 to 1, for moving up, staying and slipping; with few counts they are wide, and they narrow around the observed fractions as counts grow. Right: five horizontal stacked bars, each a sampled probability vector split into up, stay and slip; with few counts the samples differ a lot, with many counts they look alike." { const color = {domain: dir.names, range: ["#2a78d6", "#898781", "#eb6834"], legend: true}; const left = Plot.plot({width: 330, height: 240, color, x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "probability"}, y: {label: "belief density", grid: true}, style: {background: "#fcfcfb"}, marks: [Plot.line(dir.dens, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "name", strokeWidth: 2})]}); const right = Plot.plot({width: 300, height: 240, color, x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "sampled probabilities"}, y: {label: null}, style: {background: "#fcfcfb"}, marginLeft: 70, marks: [Plot.barX(dir.draws, {x: "p", y: "k", fill: "name", order: dir.names})]}); return html`

`; } ``` ## Algorithms & code ### Models from counts ::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"} ## Python ```python class MaximumLikelihoodModel: """Counts, and the maximum likelihood model they imply (eqs. 16.1-16.2): T(s2 | s, a) = N(s, a, s2) / N(s, a) and R(s, a) = rho(s, a) / N(s, a). Pairs (s, a) never tried get T = 0 and R = 0: no reward, no future.""" def __init__(self, n_states, n_actions, gamma): self.N = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions, n_states)) self.rho = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions)) self.gamma = gamma self._cache = None # (T, R) until the next update def update(self, s, a, r, s2): self.N[s, a, s2] += 1 self.rho[s, a] += r self._cache = None def counts(self): return self.N.sum(axis=2) # N(s, a) def model(self): """(T, R) as arrays; untried pairs are all zeros.""" if self._cache is None: self._cache = self._estimate() return self._cache def _estimate(self): n = self.counts() safe = np.maximum(n, 1) # avoid 0 / 0 return self.N / safe[:, :, None], self.rho / safe def q_values(self, U, s): """Q(s, a) for one state s under the model, as a vector over a.""" T, R = self.model() return R[s] + self.gamma * T[s] @ U class RmaxModel(MaximumLikelihoodModel): """R-MAX (eqs. 16.3-16.4): a pair tried fewer than m times is modeled as paying r_max forever (a self-loop), so its value is r_max / (1 - gamma) and the greedy policy is drawn toward it until it is known.""" def __init__(self, n_states, n_actions, gamma, m, r_max): super().__init__(n_states, n_actions, gamma) self.m, self.r_max = m, r_max def _estimate(self): T, R = super()._estimate() unknown = self.counts() < self.m # (S, A) mask s_idx, a_idx = np.nonzero(unknown) T[s_idx, a_idx, :] = 0.0 T[s_idx, a_idx, s_idx] = 1.0 # paired indexing: s -> s R[unknown] = self.r_max return T, R class BayesianModel: """Posterior over the model (eqs. 16.5-16.6): a Dirichlet over next states for each (s, a), starting from `prior` pseudocounts, and, because the rewards here lie in [0, 1], a Beta(1 + rho, 1 + N - rho) belief about each mean reward (fractional counts are fine).""" def __init__(self, n_states, n_actions, gamma, prior=1.0): self.alpha = np.full((n_states, n_actions, n_states), prior) self.rho = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions)) self.n = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions)) self.gamma = gamma def update(self, s, a, r, s2): self.alpha[s, a, s2] += 1 # Bayes: add the count self.rho[s, a] += r self.n[s, a] += 1 def model(self): """Posterior means: alpha normalized (eq. 16.9) and (1 + rho)/(2 + n).""" return (self.alpha / self.alpha.sum(axis=2, keepdims=True), (1 + self.rho) / (2 + self.n)) def sample(self, rng): """One MDP drawn from the posterior. A Dirichlet draw is independent gamma draws, normalized; Beta draws give the mean rewards.""" g = rng.gamma(self.alpha) T = g / g.sum(axis=2, keepdims=True) R = rng.beta(1 + self.rho, 1 + self.n - self.rho) return T, R def q_values(self, U, s): T, R = self.model() return R[s] + self.gamma * T[s] @ U ``` ## Julia ```{.julia .snippet} using ADM, Random, Statistics import Distributions p = trail() # positions 1..6, actions 1 = back, 2 = climb nS, nA, γ = size(p.R, 1), size(p.R, 2), p.γ # Counts: N[s, a, s′] transitions and ρ[s, a] reward sums. mutable struct Counts N::Array{Float64,3} ρ::Matrix{Float64} end Counts() = Counts(zeros(nS, nA, nS), zeros(nS, nA)) observe!(c::Counts, s, a, r, s′) = (c.N[s, a, s′] += 1; c.ρ[s, a] += r; c) # Maximum likelihood (eqs. 16.1-16.2); untried pairs get T = 0 and R = 0. function ml_model(c::Counts) n = max.(sum(c.N; dims = 3), 1) # N(s, a), kept as an nS × nA × 1 array; max avoids 0/0 return c.N ./ n, c.ρ ./ dropdims(n; dims = 3) end # R-MAX (eqs. 16.3-16.4): pairs tried fewer than m times loop on themselves paying rmax. function rmax_model(c::Counts; m = 10, rmax = 1.0) T, R = ml_model(c) for s in 1:nS, a in 1:nA if sum(c.N[s, a, :]) < m T[s, a, :] .= 0.0 T[s, a, s] = 1.0 R[s, a] = rmax end end return T, R end # Bayesian: Dirichlet(1 + counts) over next states, Beta(1 + ρ, 1 + N - ρ) over mean rewards. function sample_model(c::Counts, rng) n = dropdims(sum(c.N; dims = 3); dims = 3) T = zeros(nS, nA, nS) for s in 1:nS, a in 1:nA T[s, a, :] = rand(rng, Distributions.Dirichlet(1 .+ c.N[s, a, :])) end R = [rand(rng, Distributions.Beta(1 + c.ρ[s, a], 1 + n[s, a] - c.ρ[s, a])) for s in 1:nS, a in 1:nA] return T, R end # Value iteration from a warm start U (the full update). function solve!(U, T, R; tol = 1e-6) while true # Q[s, a] = R[s, a] + γ Σ_s′ T[s, a, s′] U[s′]; the sum runs over T's third axis. Q = R .+ γ .* dropdims(sum(T .* reshape(U, 1, 1, :); dims = 3); dims = 3) Unew = vec(maximum(Q; dims = 2)) done = maximum(abs.(Unew .- U)) < tol U .= Unew done && return U end end # Learn on the trail for `steps` steps: `make` builds the planning model from the counts. function run_trail(make, steps, rng; ε = 0.0) c, U, s, rewards = Counts(), zeros(nS), 1, 0.0 for t in 1:steps T, R = make(c, rng) Q = [R[s, a] + γ * sum(T[s, a, :] .* U) for a in 1:nA] a = rand(rng) < ε ? rand(rng, 1:nA) : rand(rng, findall(==(maximum(Q)), Q)) # random tie-break s′ = rand(rng, Distributions.Categorical(p.T[s, a, :])) observe!(c, s, a, p.R[s, a], s′) solve!(U, make(c, rng)...) # posterior sampling: solve a fresh sample rewards, s = t > steps - 300 ? rewards + p.R[s, a] : rewards, s′ end return rewards / 300 # average reward over the last 300 steps end learned(make; ε = 0.0) = mean(run_trail(make, 1500, MersenneTwister(seed); ε) > 0.5 for seed in 1:6) println("share learning to climb: ε-greedy ", learned((c, rng) -> ml_model(c); ε = 0.1), ", R-MAX ", learned((c, rng) -> rmax_model(c)), ", posterior sampling ", learned(sample_model)) @assert learned((c, rng) -> rmax_model(c)) > learned((c, rng) -> ml_model(c); ε = 0.1) ``` ::: ### Planners ::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"} ## Python ```python def solve(T, R, gamma, U, tol=1e-6, k_max=10_000): """Value iteration from the current U (a warm start). Updates U in place; returns the number of Bellman backups (states x sweeps).""" for k in range(1, k_max + 1): U_next = lookahead(T, R, gamma, U).max(axis=1) change = np.max(np.abs(U_next - U)) U[:] = U_next if change < tol: break return k * len(U) def full_update(model, U, s, rng=None): """Re-solve the whole estimated model after every step (16.2.1).""" T, R = model.model() return solve(T, R, model.gamma, U) def randomized_update(m): """Back up the state just left and m random states (16.2.2, Dyna-like).""" def planner(model, U, s, rng): backup(model, U, s) for s_rand in rng.integers(len(U), size=m): backup(model, U, s_rand) return m + 1 return planner def prioritized_update(m): """Prioritized sweeping (16.2.3): back up the state just left, then up to m states in order of priority. When U(s) changes by delta, each predecessor s- gets priority max over a- of T(s | s-, a-) * |delta|. The queue persists between steps, so unfinished work carries over.""" pq = {} # state -> priority def planner(model, U, s, rng): pq[s] = np.inf # the state just left first done = 0 while pq and done < m + 1: s_now = max(pq, key=pq.get) # highest priority del pq[s_now] before = U[s_now] backup(model, U, s_now) done += 1 delta = abs(U[s_now] - before) if delta == 0: continue T, _ = model.model() # T[:, :, s_now]: probability of reaching s_now from each (s-, a-). push = (T[:, :, s_now] * delta).max(axis=1) for s_pred in np.nonzero(push > 1e-12)[0]: pq[s_pred] = max(pq.get(s_pred, 0.0), push[s_pred]) return done return planner def posterior_sampling_update(model, U, s, rng): """Posterior sampling (16.6): draw an MDP from the belief, solve it, and act greedily on its values until the next update.""" T, R = model.sample(rng) return solve(T, R, model.gamma, U) ``` ## Julia ```{.julia .snippet} using ADM, Random hw = hex_world() nS, nA, γ = size(hw.R, 1), size(hw.R, 2), hw.γ # One Bellman backup of state s on the model (T, R). backup!(U, T, R, s) = (U[s] = maximum(R[s, a] + γ * sum(T[s, a, :] .* U) for a in 1:nA); U) # Prioritized sweeping: pq maps states to priorities and persists across steps. function prioritized!(U, T, R, s, pq; m = 5) pq[s] = Inf for _ in 1:m+1 isempty(pq) && break s_now = argmax(pq) # the key with the largest value delete!(pq, s_now) before = U[s_now] backup!(U, T, R, s_now) change = abs(U[s_now] - before) change == 0 && continue for s⁻ in 1:nS # predecessors: max over actions of T(s_now | s⁻, a⁻) × change priority = maximum(T[s⁻, :, s_now]) * change priority > 1e-12 && (pq[s⁻] = max(get(pq, s⁻, 0.0), priority)) end end return U end # Use the true model as a stand-in for a learned one: sweeping from the reward tiles # outward should reach the exact values with far fewer backups than full sweeps. U, pq = zeros(nS), Dict{Int,Float64}() for step in 1:400 prioritized!(U, hw.T, hw.R, rand(MersenneTwister(step), 1:nS), pq) end exact = copy(U) for _ in 1:2000 for s in 1:nS backup!(exact, hw.T, hw.R, s) end end println("mean error after 400 steps × 6 backups: ", round(sum(abs.(U .- exact)) / nS; digits = 4)) @assert sum(abs.(U .- exact)) / nS < 0.05 ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Reading the Julia code (for Python programmers)"} - **`(c.N[s, a, s′] += 1; c.ρ[s, a] += r; c)`** is a one-line function body: expressions separated by `;`, the last one returned. - **`sum(A; dims = 3)`** keeps the summed axis with length 1 (NumPy's `keepdims=True`), so `c.N ./ n` broadcasts; `dropdims` removes it. - **`reshape(U, 1, 1, :)`** turns the vector into a 1 × 1 × nS array so it lines up with T's third axis, like `U[None, None, :]`. - **`solve!(U, make(c, rng)...)`** splats the returned `(T, R)` tuple into two arguments. - **`argmax(pq)`** on a `Dict` returns the *key* with the largest value, like `max(pq, key=pq.get)`. - **`mutable struct`** fields can be reassigned; the `!` in names like `observe!` is the convention for functions that modify their arguments. ::: ### Run them ::: {#6e65e93e .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} env = trail() model = mb.RmaxModel(6, 2, env.gamma, m=10, r_max=1.0) rewards, backups, U = mb.learn(env, model, mb.full_update, 2000, 0, np.random.default_rng(0)) sampler = mb.BayesianModel(6, 2, env.gamma) rewards_ps, _, _ = mb.learn(env, sampler, mb.posterior_sampling_update, 2000, 0, np.random.default_rng(0)) ``` ::: ::: {#8c2016ec .cell execution_count=8} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R-MAX: last 500 steps average 0.852; Give the maximum likelihood $\hat T(\cdot \mid \text{kitchen}, \text{clean})$ and $\hat R(\text{kitchen}, \text{clean})$. What does the model say about (kitchen, move)? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} (kitchen, clean) was tried 3 times: to the hall twice and to the kitchen once, so $\hat T(\text{hall} \mid \text{kitchen}, \text{clean}) = 2/3$ and $\hat T(\text{kitchen} \mid \cdot) = 1/3$. The rewards were 1, 1, 0, so $\hat R = 2/3$. (kitchen, move) was never tried: with this page's convention, $\hat T = 0$ and $\hat R = 0$, a dead end worth nothing. That's pessimistic. A uniform $\hat T$, or R-MAX's optimism, would give a reason to try it. ::: **Problem 2: R-MAX's pull.** With $r_{\max} = 2$ and $\gamma = 0.9$, what is an under-tried pair worth? The agent knows a route that earns 1.5 per step forever from its current state. Where does R-MAX send it? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} An under-tried pair is modeled as paying 2 forever: $2/(1 - 0.9) = 20$. The known route is worth $1.5/(1 - 0.9) = 15$ from here. Any under-tried pair reachable soon enough, say in $k$ steps with discounted value $0.9^k \times 20 > 15$, that is $k \le 2$, beats the known route, so R-MAX goes to explore it. Farther unknowns lose to the sure 1.5 per step. Discounting limits how far optimism will travel. ::: **Problem 3: a Dirichlet update.** A state-action pair has three possible next states and a uniform prior. You observe the next states A, A, C, A, B. What is the posterior, the predictive distribution, and the probability that $\theta_A > 0.5$ roughly? (Use the Beta marginal.) ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} Posterior: $\mathrm{Dir}(1 + 3, 1 + 1, 1 + 1) = \mathrm{Dir}(4, 2, 2)$. Predictive: $4/8$, $2/8$, $2/8$. The marginal of $\theta_A$ is $\text{Beta}(4, 4)$, symmetric about 0.5, so $P(\theta_A > 0.5) = 0.5$. After many more observations at the same rates, the Beta would concentrate near 0.6 (the observed 3/5), and the probability would approach 1. ::: **Problem 4: priorities.** A backup raises $U(s)$ from 2.0 to 3.5. Under the estimated model, $s$ is reached from $s_1$ by action $a$ with probability 0.8 and by action $b$ with probability 0.1, and from $s_2$ by action $a$ with probability 0.3. $s_1$ already has priority 0.5 in the queue. What are the new priorities? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} The change is 1.5. For $s_1$, the largest transition probability into $s$ is 0.8, so the candidate is $0.8 \times 1.5 = 1.2$, and its priority becomes $\max(0.5, 1.2) = 1.2$. For $s_2$: $0.3 \times 1.5 = 0.45$. $s_1$ is backed up next. Only the most likely route into $s$ counts for each predecessor, because a change in $U(s)$ moves $s_1$'s best lookahead by at most $\gamma \times 0.8 \times 1.5$. ::: **Problem 5: why posterior sampling explores.** At the start, every pair on the trail has a uniform Dirichlet belief over the six positions. What is the predictive probability that "climb" at the trailhead leads straight to the summit? Why does that make posterior sampling explore, while the maximum likelihood agent doesn't? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"} With a uniform prior over six outcomes, the predictive probability is $1/6$. A sample often puts substantial probability on jumping far up the trail, and the reward belief, $\text{Beta}(1, 1)$, often gives the summit a high reward. So in many sampled worlds, climbing looks excellent, and the agent climbs. The maximum likelihood agent, with no data, models climbing as a dead end worth 0, and the known snack beats it. The posterior sampler's optimism fades on its own: after real climbs, the posterior concentrates on the true dynamics. ::: ## Recap 1. **Model-based learning estimates the dynamics and rewards from counts (@eq-ml, @eq-dirichlet).** *Why it matters:* a model lets every observation inform planning everywhere, which makes these methods data-efficient. Chapter 17's model-free methods trade that for less computation. 2. **The plan must follow the changing model, at a price (@eq-priority).** *Why it matters:* full replanning cost 74 backups per step on 27 states. Prioritized sweeping kept nearly the same accuracy with a handful, and full replanning's cost grows with the size of the problem. 3. **Certainty equivalence with random exploration can fail badly.** *Why it matters:* on the trail, ε-greedy stayed at the snack in 95% of runs. Rewards that require a long, deliberate trip are common in real problems, from robotics to games. 4. **Optimism drives deliberate exploration (@eq-rmax).** *Why it matters:* R-MAX travels to the unknown and has provable guarantees, but its threshold must fit the noise: too small and it trusts bad luck, too large and it explores forever. 5. **Posterior sampling explores in proportion to plausibility; the Bayes-adaptive MDP is the unreachable ideal (@eq-bamdp).** *Why it matters:* posterior sampling learned to climb in every run without tuning. The Bayes-adaptive view links learning to planning under uncertainty, the subject of Part IV. ## Cheat sheet & connections | Name | Formula | Ref | |---|---|---| | Maximum likelihood model | $\hat T = N(s, a, s')/N(s, a)$, $\hat R = \rho(s, a)/N(s, a)$ | @eq-ml | | Prioritized sweeping priority | $\max_{a^-} \hat T(s \mid s^-, a^-)\,|U(s) - u|$ | @eq-priority | | R-MAX model | under-tried: reward $r_{\max}$, self-loop; else maximum likelihood | @eq-rmax | | ★ Dirichlet posterior | $\mathrm{Dir}(\boldsymbol\alpha_0 + \mathbf N(s, a))$; predictive $\alpha(s, a, s')/\sum_{s''}\alpha(s, a, s'')$ | @eq-dirichlet | | Bayes-adaptive Bellman equation | $U^*(s, b) = \max_a (R + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s' \mid s, b, a) U^*(s', \tau(s, b, a, s')))$ | @eq-bamdp | : Key equations from this page (★ = well-known by name). {#tbl-cheatsheet} **Common pitfalls** - **Treating untried actions as bad.** A maximum likelihood model with $\hat T = 0$, $\hat R = 0$ for untried pairs makes them look worthless when rewards are positive, so they are never tried. - **Comparing planners on different data.** A planner changes the values, the values change the actions, and the actions change the data. To compare planning alone, feed every planner the same experience, as in @fig-planners. - **Resetting the priority queue.** Prioritized sweeping's leftover priorities are work still to do; discarding them each step wastes most of its advantage. - **An R-MAX threshold that is too small.** A stochastic action needs enough tries to be judged; on the trail, $m \le 3$ often gave up on the summit. - **Forgetting the cost of posterior sampling.** Solving a sampled MDP after every step is expensive in large problems; resample per episode, or plan approximately. **Connections** - [Ch 15 · Exploration and Exploitation](ch15-exploration-and-exploitation.qmd): the bandit case, Beta beliefs and Thompson sampling, which this chapter extends to many states. - [Ch 7 · Exact Solution Methods](../part2/ch07-exact-solution-methods.qmd): value iteration and Bellman backups, run here on estimated models. - [Ch 4 · Parameter Learning](../part1/ch04-parameter-learning.qmd): maximum likelihood and Dirichlet posteriors for categorical distributions. - [Ch 17 · Model-Free Methods](ch17-model-free-methods.qmd): learning values without a model, on the same trail. - [Part IV · Beliefs](../part4/ch19-beliefs.qmd): planning with beliefs, of which the Bayes-adaptive MDP is an instance.
